newsitem.title: UK: British government to fight on after majority goes.
newsitem.headline: British government to fight on after majority goes.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives suffered a crushing by-election defeat to lose their overall parliamentary majority but insisted on Friday they would struggle on in power rather than call a snap election.

"I don't think it is going to make a material difference," Prime Minister John Major told reporters in Dublin, where he is attending a European Union summit meeting. "We have been operating with a very tiny majority."
The Labour victory in the northern England seat of Barnsley East means the 323 Conservative members of parliament are matched by the same number of opposition legislators.

Labour local council leader Jeff Ennis won 14,683 votes in Barnsley East against 1,502 for Liberal Democrat David Willis and 1,299 for Conservative Jane Ellison. Turnout was a poor 33 percent of the electorate of about 53,000.
Ellison's poor showing prompted bookmakers William Hill to lengthen the odds against a Conservative general election victory to 3-1, the longest price since 1992, from 11-4.

Major must call a general election by May 22. He has hinted he will postpone polling day until the last moment in the hope improved economic conditions will persuade voters to give the Conservatives an unprecedented fifth successive term.

"I have no doubt that provided people behave themselves, we will get through to our preferred date," Major said on Friday, referring to Eurosceptic rebels in his ruling party. The Conservatives have been repeatedly split by arguments over how closely Britain should tie itself to the European Union.

"The government is going to find it increasingly a problem getting its business (through parliament)," said Donald Dewar, parliamentary business manager for Labour. "The government is now time-expired. The clock is ticking down for them."

The first major test of government support in parliament comes on Monday in a vote on the EU's fisheries policy. It lost a similar vote last year by two and has ordered all its MPs to attend to avoid a similar fiasco.

The position of the government, 21 points behind Labour in the last national opinion poll, was weakened last week when one of its legislators, Sir John Gorst, said he could no longer promise Major his automatic support because of a row over hospital facilities in his North London constituency.
But the Conservatives are optimistic it will prove difficult for Labour to unite all the opposition parties against the government in key Commons votes.
In particular, they hope the nine MPs who represent the Ulster Unionist party which seeks to preserve British rule over Northern Ireland will hesitate to turn them out of office.
The final test of public opinion before the general election could come in a by-election in the north-western seat of Wirral South following the death of Conservative Barry Porter.

If the Conservatives were to lose this seat, which Porter won with an 8,183 vote majority at the 1992 general election, it would also lose its majority in key parliamentary committees, making governing still more difficult.

The Barnsley by-election was a setback for the Socialist Labour Party set up by miners' union leader Arthur Scargill in protest at Labour's abandonment of traditional left-wing policy stances under moderate leader Tony Blair.

Its candidate, Ken Capstick won only 949 votes, just over five percent of the total. Ennis was defending a Labour majority of 24,777 votes won by his predecessor Terry Patchett, whose recent death led to the by-election.
